title: Internationalizing IPv6 Using 128-Bit Unicode
summary: This is an April 1st humor RFC. It jokes that Unicode will run out of code points and that the next size will be 128 bits, then suggests ways to link that to IPv6 addresses. It should not be read as a real proposal.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke proposes treating Unicode code points as IPv6 addresses. It imagines addresses shown as symbols and proposes related naming and routing ideas.

subtitle: An April 1st joke imagines using 128-bit Unicode code points as IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke imagines Unicode exhausting its code points and proposes a 128-bit space that matches IPv6 address size.
tldr.mechanism: It describes IPv6 addresses as Unicode code points, with glyphs, short-name tags, multicast forms and an imagined resolution system.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational humor document, not a real proposal to change Unicode or IPv6.

today: RFC 8369 is an Informational April 1st joke document. It should not be treated as a real proposal for Unicode or IPv6.

sections.title: The 128-Bit Unicode Premise
sections.content:
RFC 8369 is an April 1st humor document. It imagines that Unicode will exhaust its code points and that the next code point size will be 128 bits, then connects that imagined change to IPv6.

The RFC says Unicode expansion details are outside its scope. It follows the assumption of a future fixed-length UTF-128 encoding and presents the rest of the document as a way to use it for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an April 1st joke about a future 128-bit Unicode. The document connects that imagined size to the 128-bit length of IPv6 addresses.

sections.title: Unicode IPv6 Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC proposes representing IPv6 addresses as Unicode code points. It suggests that users could enter glyphs instead of hexadecimal addresses, and gives textual forms such as a U+ prefixed representation or a short-name tag.

It defines humorous terms for code points representing individuals, aliens, unknown things and obfuscated identities. It also suggests reserving the high-order bit for multicast groups.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal would let an address appear as a Unicode character or a short-name tag. It also assigns imagined meanings to different classes of symbols.

sections.title: Allocation and Resolution
sections.content:
The RFC imagines replacing DNS with a Code Point Unicode Resolution System, or CPURS, to map code points to glyphs and short-name tags. It says registrations would replace IANA and Regional Internet Registry allocations in this imagined model.

These proposals are presented as part of the joke. The RFC also proposes using an omoji by setting the least-significant bit to obfuscate an address, while acknowledging this provides only a bit of privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC imagines a new system to register and look up Unicode addresses. It also proposes an address marker for obfuscation, while saying the privacy is limited.
